story1034:
In Abenaki tradition, the Great Spirit Tabaldak first created the world and all the people. When he finished making humans, he wiped the dust from his hands, and from this divine dust were born twin brothers — Glooscap (also called Gluskabe) and Malsumis.

Glooscap was good and creative. He shaped the mountains and rivers, the forests and meadows. He made the animals and taught them to live in harmony with the people. He created the seasons — spring, summer, autumn, winter — so that the world would be ever-changing, ever-renewing.

Malsumis was destructive and jealous. He made the wolves and the serpents, the thorns and the poison ivy. He created the storms and the earthquakes, the droughts and the floods. He was angry that his brother's creations were loved and his were feared.

The brothers fought. Glooscap defeated Malsumis and banished him to the underworld. But Malsumis's creations remained — the wolves still howl, the serpents still strike, the storms still rage. They are the necessary counterbalance to Glooscap's goodness.

Tabaldak watched the conflict between his sons and was satisfied. The world needed both — the creative force of Glooscap and the destructive force of Malsumis. Without destruction, there could be no renewal. Without darkness, light would have no meaning.

The Abenaki tell this story to explain the dual nature of existence — the presence of both good and evil, creation and destruction, in every aspect of life.
story1035:
In the time of the first people, the Abenaki were hungry. Gluskabe's grandmother Nokomes taught the people to survive on wild plants, but food was scarce. First Mother, the first woman created by Gichish Kizos, the Great Spirit, saw that the people were suffering.

First Mother gathered the people together and told them she was going to sacrifice herself so that they could eat. She lay down on the ground and asked the people to bury her. They did as she asked, covering her body with earth and mourning her passing.

From her grave, corn grew. The stalks were tall and green, the ears full and golden. The people harvested the corn and cooked it, and they were hungry no more.

First Mother had given her life so that the people could live. The corn was her body, the kernels her children, the silk her hair. To eat corn was to remember her sacrifice, to honor her gift.

The Abenaki tell this story to explain why corn is the most sacred of all plants. It is not merely food — it is the body of First Mother, the first woman, the mother of all. When the people plant corn, they are tending her memory. When they harvest it, they are accepting her gift.

The story teaches that the greatest sacrifices are made by those who love us most, and that the gifts of the earth are the gifts of the spirits.
story1036:
Gluskonba (Glooscap) offered four Abenaki men a single wish each. The first man wished to be powerful and rich, and was turned into a great pine tree — tall and strong, but rooted in one place forever.

The second man wished to be swift and free, and was turned into a hawk — able to fly anywhere, but unable to speak or think.

The third man wished to be wise and respected, and was turned into a beaver — building great dams, but unable to share his knowledge with others.

The fourth man wished for nothing. He said, "I am content as I am. I have my family, my home, my people. What more could I want?"

Gluskonba smiled. "You are the wisest of all," he said. "The pine tree is tall but cannot move. The hawk is swift but cannot speak. The beaver is wise but cannot teach. You alone have everything — strength in your limbs, freedom in your heart, wisdom in your mind, and love in your life."

The story teaches that contentment is the greatest wisdom, and that the desire for more is the root of all suffering. The fourth man understood what the others did not — that happiness comes not from having more but from appreciating what you already have.
